cards.heading: Threat, vulnerability, exploit, mitigation
cards.body: A vulnerability is a weakness (unpatched software, a default password). A threat is something that could take advantage of it. An exploit is the actual technique or code that does. Mitigation reduces the risk: patching, hardening, filtering, monitoring.

cards.heading: The CIA triad
cards.body: Security protects confidentiality (only the right people can read data), integrity (data isn't changed without detection) and availability (systems are there when needed). Attacks target one or more of them: eavesdropping hits confidentiality, tampering integrity, DoS availability. Encryption protects confidentiality; a hash of a file, checked later, shows it hasn't changed, which protects integrity; redundancy protects availability.

cards.heading: Denial of service
cards.body: DoS overwhelms a target so legitimate users can't reach it. DDoS uses many sources, often a botnet. Reflection attacks spoof the victim's address in requests to third-party servers; amplification picks requests whose replies are much bigger (DNS, NTP), multiplying the flood. A TCP SYN flood opens many half-finished three-way handshakes, so the server waits on half-open connections until it can't accept real ones.

cards.heading: Spoofing and man-in-the-middle
cards.body: Spoofing fakes an identity: a source IP, a MAC address or a rogue DHCP server. A man-in-the-middle sits between two parties to read or alter traffic, for example with ARP poisoning (fake ARP replies mapping the gateway's IP to the attacker's MAC). A man-in-the-middle (on-path) attacker relays the traffic, so both victims think they're talking to each other directly. ARP spoofing and rogue DHCP servers are common ways to get into the path.

cards.heading: Reconnaissance and malware
cards.body: Reconnaissance gathers information before an attack: ping sweeps, port scans, public records. Malware: a virus attaches to files and spreads when they run; a worm spreads by itself across the network; a trojan pretends to be useful software; ransomware encrypts data for a ransom.

cards.heading: Social engineering
cards.body: Attacks on people rather than systems. Phishing (mass email), spear phishing (targeted), whaling (executives), vishing (voice), smishing (SMS), pretexting (a made-up story) and tailgating (following someone through a secured door).

cards.heading: Password attacks
cards.body: Guessing (common passwords), dictionary attacks (word lists), brute force (every combination) and credential stuffing (passwords leaked elsewhere). Defences: long passwords, lockouts, MFA and never reusing passwords.
